title: How to Build an AI Agent That Actually Works in Production
excerpt: Most AI agent demos impress in a controlled environment and fail in production. Here is the engineering discipline that separates demos from systems people depend on.
body:
The gap between a working AI agent demo and a production AI agent is larger than most teams expect. A demo runs against clean data, predictable inputs, and a single user. A production agent runs against messy data, unexpected inputs, and a hundred users who will find every edge case you did not think of.

Here is the engineering discipline that closes that gap.

## Start with the failure modes, not the success path

Every AI agent project should begin by answering one question: **what happens when the agent is wrong?**

Not if — when. The agent will be wrong. The question is whether your system handles it gracefully or catastrophically.

Three failure modes to design for from day one:

1. **Hallucination.** The agent generates confident, plausible, incorrect information. The fix is not "better prompts" — it is retrieval over verified data, confidence thresholds, and human review for high-stakes outputs.
2. **Ambiguity.** The input could mean multiple things, and the agent picks the wrong interpretation. The fix is a clarification loop: when confidence is low, ask the user to confirm before acting.
3. **System failure.** The API the agent calls is down, the database is unreachable, or the model times out. The fix is retry logic with exponential backoff, graceful degradation, and clear error messages to the user.

## The architecture that survives production

A production AI agent has five layers, and each one matters:

### 1. Input handling
Accept structured and unstructured input. Parse emails, form submissions, chat messages, and API calls into a common format before the agent sees them. The agent should never deal with raw HTTP requests or email MIME types.

### 2. Retrieval
The agent needs access to your data — knowledge base articles, CRM records, product information, policies. Use a vector store for semantic search and a structured database for exact lookups. Never rely on the model's training data for your business information.

### 3. Reasoning
This is where the model sits. But the model should not operate alone — wrap it in an evaluation harness that tests every prompt against known inputs and expected outputs. Run these tests on every deployment.

### 4. Action
The agent should be able to do things: create tickets, update records, send messages, call APIs. Each action needs:
- **Permissions** — what the agent is allowed to do
- **Idempotency** — doing the same action twice should not create duplicates
- **Audit trail** — every action logged with who, what, when, and why

### 5. Observation
Log everything. Transcripts, model calls, latency, error rates, user feedback. Without observation, you cannot improve the agent — and you will not know when it degrades.

## The evaluation harness

This is the piece most teams skip, and it is the piece that determines whether the agent stays reliable over time.

An evaluation harness is a test suite for your AI agent. It consists of:

- **Test cases:** Known inputs with expected outputs. "When a user asks about pricing, the agent should reference the pricing page, not make up numbers."
- **Regression tests:** Run on every prompt change. If a prompt update breaks one test case, it does not ship.
- **Quality metrics:** Track accuracy, response time, and user satisfaction over time. Set thresholds and alert when they drop.

We run evaluation harnesses for every agent we build. The first version takes a day to set up. The ongoing cost is a few hours per month. The alternative — discovering your agent has been giving wrong answers for three weeks — is far more expensive.

## The monitoring stack

Production agents need:

- **Real-time alerts** when error rates spike or latency exceeds thresholds
- **Transcript review** — someone should read a sample of conversations weekly
- **Drift detection** — track whether the agent's accuracy is declining over time
- **Cost monitoring** — model API costs can surprise you if usage grows unexpectedly

Set up monitoring before you launch, not after the first incident.

## The handover

The agent should be maintainable by someone who did not build it. That means:

- **Architecture documentation** that explains why each decision was made
- **Runbooks** for common failure scenarios
- **Configuration** that lives in files or a CMS, not hardcoded in prompts
- **Tests** that verify the agent works correctly after changes

If your agent can only be maintained by the specific engineer who built it, you have a single point of failure, not a production system.

## A realistic timeline

Here is what a production-quality AI agent actually takes:

| Phase | Duration | What happens |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Discovery | 1–2 weeks | Map the workflow, define failure behaviour, identify data sources |
| Architecture | 1 week | Design the retrieval, reasoning, and action layers |
| Build | 3–6 weeks | Implement the agent, integrations, and evaluation harness |
| Testing | 1–2 weeks | Red-teaming, edge case testing, performance validation |
| Launch | 1 week | Staged rollout with monitoring |
| Stabilisation | 4–6 weeks | Tune based on real transcripts, fix edge cases |

Total: 8–14 weeks for a workflow agent. Longer for voice or multi-agent systems.

## The honest answer

Building an AI agent that works in production is an engineering project, not a research project. It requires the same discipline you would apply to any production system: testing, monitoring, documentation, and a plan for what happens when things go wrong.
